color_change:
Compared with the previous frame, the tablet shows increased exposure of a yellow inner layer (localized dome on top and yellow staining on the upper side) while the original pink outer coating has been eroded into loose pink powder that accumulates at the base. Color change is localized to the tablet and immediate vicinity (pink powder ring, yellow dome and yellow residues on the rim); the bulk dissolution medium remains visually dark/clear with only small bright bubbles/particles near the tablet rather than a diffused color throughout the vessel.

---

The tablet shows a two-tone appearance: a pink/red core with a bright yellow-green fluffy layer on top. Compared to the previous frame the yellow region has spread slightly laterally and appears marginally more intense (more area covered), while the pink core remains visible. There is no noticeable coloration of the bulk medium - color release is localized to the tablet surface and the immediate powder pile at the base (no diffuse yellowing of the surrounding liquid or background).

---

Overall bulk colors (red/orange core with a yellow-green top coating and pink powder at the base) are preserved relative to the previous frame. The most notable color redistribution at the current timepoint is a small increase in exposed orange material (a detached orange fragment visible above the tablet) and slightly more yellow-green coating material smeared toward the upper side walls. No diffuse coloration of the surrounding medium is observed - color change is localized to the tablet surface and the immediate powder halo.

---

Tablet remains dominantly orange-red with a persistent white powdery layer and small yellow/beige cores on the top. Compared with the previous frame, there is noticeably more diffuse red/orange material released around the tablet - the red pigment has formed a dense, fuzzy cloud and a laterally spreading red layer at the tablet base. The color release is localized around the tablet (halo and upward/forward plume) rather than uniformly tinting the whole vessel.

---

Compared with the previous frame, the tablet shows an increased exposure of yellow material at the top while the original pink outer layer is losing pigment and producing pink powder at the base. Color is now bi-modal (yellow dome + remaining pink ring) rather than predominantly pink. The medium remains visually colorless/clear - color from the tablet is localized near the tablet and as a concentrated ring of suspended/settled pink powder immediately around the tablet rather than diffused throughout the entire vessel.

---

Tablet shows a two-tone appearance: red/orange core with a yellow-green, powdery/foamy layer developing on the crown. Compared with the previous frame, the yellow-green layer appears slightly more extensive and slightly greener in places; there is no visible color diffusion into the surrounding medium - the vessel remains optically clear/black in the background. No overall medium coloration or large cloud of dissolved pigment is observed; color change is localized on the tablet surface.

---

Top-of-tablet colours remain strongly localized: a yellow-green hydrated/soft layer sits on the tablet crown while the core body stays red/orange and a pink powder ring accumulates at the base. There is no visible colour diffusion into the surrounding medium - colour change is local to the tablet surface and freshly detached powder.

---

The tablet and released material are strongly orange-red. Compared with the previous frame, the red color is more diffuse and extended laterally - a dense red cloud now occupies the right/lower quadrant in front of the tablet. The tablet top still shows a white/pale crust with small yellow-green specks that remain localized to the tablet surface; however the orange pigment that was previously confined to the tablet body is now spreading into the surrounding area.
shape_change:
The overall outline has become more irregular versus the previous frame: the once-regular cylindrical outline is now eroded at the rim with a bulging yellow dome on top and missing material around the edge. Progression is intact → partial rim loss and delamination → irregular remnant with asymmetric top bulge and loose fragments at the base.

---

Overall cylindrical outline of the tablet base is still intact, but the upper profile is more irregular than in the previous frame. The most critical change versus the previous timepoint is increased irregularity of the top surface (the yellow layer has become more spread and ragged), indicating continued breakdown of the original smooth crown into an irregular, porous cap rather than complete fragmentation into many large pieces.

---

The tablet core remains essentially cylindrical and largely intact, but compared with the previous frame there is a clear discrete fragmentation event: a small, nearly cylindrical/orbicular piece has detached and is now separated above the tablet surface. The overall outline of the main tablet is still continuous (no complete break-up), but the top profile is more irregular where material has been lost.

---

The original cylindrical outline is still partially recognizable but is progressively losing definition. Compared with the previous frame the critical change is a larger lateral smear and loss of a clean lower edge - the tablet is transitioning from an intact/partially eroded disk to a central core with an irregular surrounding mass and an extended plume. No numerous large discrete fragments are evident; instead the solid is breaking into a cohesive smear and fine particulate cloud.

---

The overall cylindrical outline is still recognizable but more irregular than the previous frame: the top now has a raised yellow dome and the peripheral rim is eroded. The tablet has progressed from mostly intact to partially missing outer material and emerging irregular fragments; the critical change vs the previous frame is further rim erosion and a clearer pyramidal/peaked top rather than a smooth cap.

---

The overall circular outline of the tablet base remains largely intact (no full breakup into major fragments), but the rim and top profile have become more irregular. Compared to the previous timepoint there is incremental loss of a defined crisp edge at the top rim and small pieces of the coating/material have detached, producing a ragged silhouette rather than a perfectly rounded cap.

---

Overall cylindrical outline of the tablet is still present but no longer a single smooth disk - the rim is eroded and small chunks have separated. Compared with the previous frame the critical change is a discrete detached pellet/fragment that is now separated above the tablet (an ejection event); prior to that the tablet was intact aside from rim erosion. The progression is intact → rim erosion and powdering → discrete fragment detachment/ejection.

---

The tablet core remains largely recognizable as a rounded disk, but the outline is becoming irregular. Compared to the previous timepoint the right flank has lost a clearer boundary and a large, arching filament of particulate material has formed and bent over the tablet; the overall shape has progressed from an intact/partially eroded disk toward a disk with an extended, trailing plume and smeared lateral fragments.
surface_texture_change:
Surface roughness has increased relative to the previous image. The outer surface shows more flaky/crusty powder and a crumbly texture at the rim; the yellow region looks smoother and swollen/pasty in contrast to the coarse pink debris. Small adherent bubbles and fine particulate on the surface are new compared to the prior frame.

---

Surface texture has become fuzzier and more porous compared with the previous frame: the yellow top appears more granular/flocculent and small surface particles are more apparent. The previously smoother rim shows increased micro-roughness and more discrete powdering; no large cracks are visible but the surface is clearly transitioning from compact to friable.

---

Surface has become visibly more granular and rough relative to the previous image; the top coating shows a loose, crumbly texture with fine particles and small clumps. Edges of the top layer appear eroded with micro-flaky debris; the side wall remains textured with adhered granules. The largest change versus the prior frame is the appearance of loosened granules and a disrupted top crust where the fragment separated.

---

Surface has evolved from visibly granular to a very fuzzy, fibrous appearance where particles are suspended in a plume. The white top layer remains crumbly, but the sidewalls now exhibit a wet-looking, matte-to-fuzzy texture with many fine particles detaching. Compared to the prior frame there is increased surface disaggregation (more fine particulate suspension and a softer, fuzz-like exterior).

---

Surface has become much rougher versus the previous frame: granular, chalky powdering at the edges and a visibly friable texture where the pink coating has sloughed off. Small clumps and a discontinuous crust are present; the yellow region appears smoother but still porous. No large cracks are visible, but progressive granular disintegration is obvious compared to the prior image.

---

Surface has transitioned from smooth-coated to rough/crusty with a granular, fluffy appearance on the crown. Small crystalline/granular deposits and fine powder adhere to the sides and top. Relative to the previous image the crown texture is slightly more fibrillar/crumbly and the fine powder coating on the sidewall is denser - more high-frequency roughness and visible friable particles.

---

Surface texture has become markedly granular and flaky compared with the previous frame. The crown shows a softer, crumbly, almost flock-like yellow/green layer and many small high-contrast granules on the red body indicate surface break-up and flaking. New loose powder and roughness are visibly increased relative to the prior image.

---

Surface texture has become much fuzzier and granular. The previous frame showed a relatively rough but compact surface; the current frame shows increased fluffy, fibrous appearance at the emerging plume and more powdery erosion at the tablet rim. The white crust on top appears more crumbly with exposed yellow-green granules.
volume_change:
Net material at the original cylinder footprint appears reduced (base material has sloughed off into a surrounding powder mound) while the top shows a localized swelling (yellow dome). Overall occupied solid mass is decreasing laterally even though the top shows a small swollen protrusion.

---

Projected height and overall occupied footprint are approximately stable but the top has flattened slightly as the yellow material spreads - this suggests limited net volume loss so far with redistribution (slight collapse/settling of the top layer) rather than a large decrease in total volume between the two frames.

---

Projected area and apparent height of the main core remain approximately constant - no gross swelling or collapse is evident. However there is a slight reduction of material at the top (local loss of coating) consistent with a small net decrease in tablet volume at the topmost region compared to the previous frame.

---

Projected height of the central core is roughly maintained but the lateral projected volume has increased substantially as red material spreads outwards. Compared with the previous frame, the most important trend is lateral expansion (apparent loss of compactness) rather than a marked reduction in central height - the tablet appears to be collapsing outward into a thin, spreading mass.

---

Projected volume appears marginally reduced at the base (loss of material into powder) while the top shows a local bulge (yellow dome) - net apparent height is similar or slightly increased locally but bulk mass near the base is reduced by erosion. Overall trend since earlier frames is outer-layer mass loss (decreasing effective volume of the compact ring) with local swelling/extrusion at the core/top.

---

Projected height and gross volume of the solid core appear approximately conserved; however there is clear net mass redistribution from the tablet into a ring of loose powder at the base. There is no obvious swelling-then-collapse behavior visible here - the dominant qualitative trend is surface erosion and loss of cohesive volume into a surrounding powder bed rather than a dramatic shrinkage of the core.

---

Projected volume of the main tablet body is approximately similar to the previous frame, but there is a small net loss of material from the crown (seen as powder at the base and the detached fragment). No evidence of a prior swelling-then-collapse cycle at this stage; trend is slow net material loss with local collapse at the crown.

---

Projected height of the central disk is similar or slightly reduced while the lateral projected area has increased substantially. Relative to the previous frame the tablet has redistributed mass outward - apparent local volume at the core is decreasing while a low-profile, high-area cloud/film of material has formed on the surface and along the substrate.
dissolution_speed_time:
Disintegration is ongoing. Compared with the previous frame there is no single catastrophic breakup but continued surface erosion and increased powder shedding - i.e., steady erosion rather than a sudden acceleration event. The most critical change is increased rim delamination and powder release with concurrent appearance of surface bubbles.

---

Disintegration/dissolution appears ongoing but not rapidly accelerating at this point. Compared to the previous frame the process shows steady continuation (spreading of top material and more adhered bubbles) rather than a sudden fragmentation event; therefore the instantaneous rate is moderate and likely decelerating compared with earlier stage(s) in the sequence.

---

Relative to the previous timepoint, disintegration is showing a momentary acceleration marked by a sudden detachment of a discrete fragment. Prior to this the tablet appeared to be eroding slowly; the current frame indicates a stage-wise jump (local mechanical/structural failure) rather than a steady slow dissolution.

---

Disintegration appears to be accelerating at the current timepoint relative to the previous frame: particle shedding and plume density have increased and a rapid lateral spread of material is evident. The sequence suggests a stage-wise shift from slow surface erosion to faster bulk surface breakdown and mass sloughing at this interval.

---

Disintegration rate appears to be steady to slightly accelerating at this timepoint compared with the previous frame: more powder has detached and the rim shows increased material loss. The most critical change is faster peripheral erosion and increased particulate release since the previous image, indicating a burst/accelerated erosion stage.

---

Disintegration is proceeding steadily but not explosively. Compared with the previous frame, the rate of visible particle detachment and powder accumulation at the base has increased slightly but remains gradual - no sudden fragmentation or rapid turbidity spike is seen between these two frames. The most critical change is incremental increase in powder release and surface fracturing.

---

Disintegration rate appears to have accelerated at this time point compared with the immediately previous image - the most critical change is the sudden detachment/ejection of a fragment, accompanied by increased powder at the base. This indicates a stage-wise step: steady surface erosion followed by a sudden fragmentation event.

---

Disintegration appears to be accelerating at this timepoint: the amount of loose particulate and the extent of the red cloud increased markedly compared to the previous image, indicating a rapid release/erosion phase rather than steady slow dissolution.
physical_state_change:
The tablet interior/top appears to transition toward a looser, more paste-like/swollen state (yellow region) while the outer layer has become friable granular powder. The structure is becoming looser and partially collapsed at the rim compared with the previous frame.

---

The top layer is transitioning from a compact coating to a loose, swollen/flocculent mass (soft porous aggregate). There is no complete transition to a paste or fully suspended fine-particle cloud yet - instead the internal structure at the surface is loosening and producing free powder that accumulates at the base.

---

Top layer is transitioning from a cohesive coating to a looser, powdery/granular state; internal core remains solid and intact. The critical change vs the previous frame is a local transition to detached solid granule(s) (one larger fragment plus many fine particulates) indicating localized structural breakdown rather than full gelation or complete collapse.

---

There is a clear transition from a solid/granular tablet to a loosened, partially cohesive, paste-like/very fine particulate state. Compared with the prior frame the internal structure appears looser and more disrupted, with formation of a fluffy plume and a wet-like smear indicating partial conversion to a slurry or highly hydrated particulate mass.

---

The solid surface is transitioning to a loose, friable granular state at the exterior while the interior/top region is swollen or softened (yellow, dome-like). Internal structure is becoming looser with clear structural breakdown at the outer layer - the tablet is moving from compact solid toward a two-phase state (soft/swollen core + particulate crust).

---

The tablet interior surface is becoming looser and more friable; the crown shows a transition toward a crumbly, sponge-like aggregate. The material appears to be breaking down into coarse powder and small granules rather than converting into a fully gel-like or pasty state at this timepoint.

---

The tablet surface has transitioned from a cohesive solid to a looser, crumbly/particulate state at the crown. The detached fragment and abundant powder show conversion to discrete solid particles rather than a homogeneous gel or paste; internal structure appears more porous and mechanically weakened.

---

The dominant change is solid → dispersed particulate/fuzzy aggregate. The tablet interior still shows solid granules (yellow-green beads), but much of the outer material has transitioned to loose, airborne/suspended micro-particles or a fluffy paste-like layer; there is no indication of a clear gel - instead a dry/colloidal particulate cloud is forming.
dissolution_medium:
The medium remains largely clear; however, there are more small suspended bubbles and very local suspended particles around the tablet compared with the prior frame. No large-scale turbidity or cloud-like dispersion is visible - changes are spatially localized near the tablet surface.

---

The background medium remains optically clear (black backdrop + clear liquid appearance) with only a few small suspended specks visible. There is no large-scale turbidity or colored clouding; particulates are confined near the tablet. Given the neutral observation, the medium does not show evidence of bulk saturation or widespread particle dispersion at this time.

---

The background/medium remains visually clear (black background) with no obvious turbidity or coloration spreading into the bulk medium. All particulate matter is confined near the tablet; there is no visible clouding or streaking in the surrounding medium compared to the previous frame.

---

The background medium is visually dark (no overall coloration of the vessel), but locally the immediate medium around the tablet shows dense suspended red particles (cloud/plume) and a turbid-looking layer at the base. Compared with the previous frame local turbidity and suspended particle density have increased; there is no evidence that the entire vessel is uniformly tinted yet - effects remain spatially concentrated.

---

The bulk medium remains visually clear/black background in the frame; turbidity is localized to a dense cloud of pink powder immediately adjacent to the tablet surface and some small suspended particles/bubbles around the tablet. There is no large scale coloration of the medium - suspended particles are concentrated near the tablet suggesting limited dispersion so far.

---

The medium (visual field) remains clear with no large-scale turbidity or colored clouding. Small adherent air/solution bubbles cling to the tablet surface; otherwise there are no streaks, precipitation bands, or suspended clouds visible. The clear medium suggests limited release of colored soluble species into the bulk (color effects are localized at the tablet surface).

---

The surrounding medium (visible background and vessel surface) remains visually clear and black in the images; there is no detectable turbidity or colouration spreading into the medium. Released material remains as visible particulate/powder on the vessel surface rather than dispersed as a diffuse cloud.

---

The background is dark (no visible colored bulk solvent); turbidity is manifested as a local red particulate cloud rather than uniform medium coloration. Compared with the previous frame the particulate cloud density and spatial extent in the medium/substrate interface increased, producing a continuous red smear over the grid surface.
fragment_distribution_density:
Fragments remain concentrated around the original tablet position, forming a dense ring of pink powder at the base and some adhered fines on the tablet side. Fragment count/visible powder density has increased since the previous frame but fragments are still locally confined rather than uniformly dispersed across the vessel.

---

Fragments and fines are concentrated around the tablet base in a localized powder halo; fragment density appears slightly increased relative to the previous frame (more fine powder piled at the contact plane), but fragments remain coarse-to-fine and clustered rather than uniformly dispersed. A few adhered bubbles on the tablet edge are larger in the current frame, but there is no widespread suspension of many small fragments throughout the vessel.

---

Fragments remain concentrated around the tablet base and top: a rim of pink powder at the base and multiple fine particles on the tablet flank. Compared with the previous timepoint, fragment density at the very top has increased (appearance of a detached orange piece), while lateral spread is still localized - no uniform dispersion throughout the vessel. Particle sizes range from fine powder to a single distinct larger fragment visible above the tablet.

---

Fragments are concentrated at and just outside the original tablet perimeter: a dense bed of fine powder beneath the tablet and a thick cloud/plume up and away from the core. Compared with the previous frame fragment density has increased (more fine particulates in the plume and a broader lateral dispersion). There are many fine particles rather than a few large chunks; some sedimentation is visible directly under the tablet while a higher-density suspended region sits adjacent to it.

---

Fragmentation is concentrated at the tablet perimeter: a ring/patch of fine pink powder and small clumps sits on the support surface around the tablet. Fragment density near the tablet has increased since the previous frame (more powder and larger clumps), but fragments are not yet uniformly dispersed in the vessel. Few discrete larger particles are visible; most material is fine, high local density at the base.

---

Detached fragments and powder are concentrated at the tablet base forming a circumferential pile; few small particles adhere to the sidewalls. Compared with the previous image the pile at the base is marginally larger and denser, with more fine dust present. Fragments are not yet uniformly dispersed in the vessel - high local particle density at the base vs near-zero density elsewhere.

---

Fragments and powder are concentrated immediately around the tablet base forming a ring of pink powder; particle density at the tablet perimeter has increased since the previous frame. A single larger fragment is now detached and suspended above the tablet centre (newly formed), while smaller granules remain locally clustered rather than uniformly dispersed across the field.

---

Fragments and powder are concentrated immediately around the tablet base and spreading to the right; fragment density near the tablet perimeter has increased since the previous frame (more fine particles and a denser cloud). There is a clear local accumulation on the substrate beneath and ahead of the tablet rather than a uniform dispersion across the field.
output_text:
Step 1 — Experimental background & setup
User input - We are analyzing the static disintegration images of two Nifedipine Controlled-Release Tablets. All images were captured under the same experimental conditions. The dissolution medium is a phosphate buffer at pH 6.8, and the experiment was conducted at a controlled temperature of 38 °C to simulate a slightly elevated physiological condition. The total observation period is 36hs. Images were captured continuously and later sampled into batches. Each message you receive contains multiple images representing a time window (e.g., 0–9h, 9–18 h， 18–27h , 27–36h). Treat the images within the same window as observations from that time range rather than a single exact time point. Please treat all images as coming from the same batch and formulation of gliclazide tablets, and use this background information when interpreting the disintegration behavior and describing the eight dimensions of disintegration.

Release is designed to be largely independent of pH and GI motility; expect minimal pH-dependence in release profile, but membrane integrity, orifice behavior, and push-layer hydration/swelling are critical for visual disintegration signatures.” }, “drug_2”: { “api”: null, “dosage_form”: null, “excipients”: [], “key_comments”: “No second drug specified.” } }, “analysis_plan”: { “dimensions”: [ “Color Change”, “Shape Change”, “Surface Texture Change”, “Volume Change”, “Dissolution Speed and Time”, “Physical State Change”, “Dissolution Medium”, “Fragment Distribution with Density” ], “single_drug_strategy”: “Preprocess all images (dark-frame subtraction, white-balance, geometric alignment, scale calibration). Define a fixed region of interest (ROI) around the tablet. For each timepoint extract quantitative metrics: (1) Color Change — compute color histograms and delta-E in a consistent color space (e.g., CIELAB) vs t0; (2) Shape Change — segment tablet silhouette, compute contour, area, perimeter, aspect ratio, circularity, convex-hull metrics and track changes over time; (3) Surface Texture Change — use texture descriptors (GLCM contrast/correlation/entropy, local binary patterns, high-frequency energy) to detect surface swelling, cracking or membrane disruption; (4) Volume Change — estimate projected area and, if multi-view or known geometry, approximate volume; alternatively use wetting-induced translucency changes as surrogate for mass loss; (5) Dissolution Speed and Time — derive percent area remaining curve, time-to-x% area loss (e.g., t50), slope of area decline, and correlate with intensity-based dissolved fraction if dye/pigment available; (6) Physical State Change — detect events like membrane swelling, push-layer extrusion, or orifice formation via morphological event detectors (sudden area jumps, edge discontinuities); (7) Dissolution Medium — monitor background turbidity and color (image of blank vessel as control) to detect suspended fragments or particle release; (8) Fragment Distribution with Density — perform particle segmentation on each frame for detached fragments, measure count, size distribution, and spatial density (fragments per unit area) and track temporal evolution. Apply smoothing and noise filtering to time series, and compute confidence intervals from replicate vessels.”, “two_drug_comparison_strategy”: “Compute the same set of quantitative time-series metrics for both groups and normalize to initial values to enable direct comparison. Compare key summary metrics: time-to-event (e.g., membrane rupture), t50 or t90 (area or mass surrogate), initial slope (rate), AUC of area remaining curve, peak fragment count and time-to-peak. Use paired plots of metric vs time, difference curves, and statistical tests (e.g., repeated-measures ANOVA or nonparametric equivalent) across replicates to assess significance. For morphology-based differences, compare distributions of shape descriptors and texture metrics (Kolmogorov–Smirnov or permutation tests). Visualize with heatmaps (metrics × time), aligned event markers, and clustering of time-series trajectories to identify distinct dissolution patterns. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals and, where relevant, correlate optical metrics to orthogonal dissolution or mass-loss measurements.” } }

Higher-viscosity HPMC typically produces a thicker, more cohesive gel that swells more slowly but resists erosion longer, shifting release toward polymer relaxation/diffusion control rather than immediate erosion. This behaviour is well described in the controlled‑release literature (Siepmann/Peppas and others).

They also promote heterogeneous microstructure (islands of hydrophobic phase), which changes mechanical breakup patterns.
- Film coating composition, thickness and permeability determine whether the outer coat dissolves, ruptures, or remains intact and simply permeable: insoluble but permeable coatings allow water ingress (leading to core swelling) but keep outer shell intact; plasticizer content, curing/annealing and coating porosity influence film brittleness/cracking and gas/vapor permeability. Enteric or insoluble coatings can therefore produce long-lived swollen cores beneath an intact shell.

In osmotic systems, core swelling creates internal pressure — filled or small orifices can lead to shell retention with surface bulging.

Surface properties (hydrophilicity, presence of surfactant) influence whether fragments aggregate, float, or sink.

Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - Hydrophilic matrix polymers (HPMC): Multiple studies show that higher-viscosity grades and higher HPMC content produce a thicker, more cohesive gel layer that swells but resists erosion, slowing disintegration and drug release. Lower-viscosity grades form weaker gels that erode/disintegrate faster (typical observation across in vitro dissolution studies).
- Hydrophobic excipients/lipids: Incorporation of hydrophobic materials (e.g., glyceryl behenate, stearates, waxes) reduces wettability and water penetration, promoting core swelling without rapid disintegration and often producing buoyant or slow-eroding fragments. Hydrophobic coatings or core lipids can also reduce dissolution rate and fragment erosion.
- Film-coating properties: Coating polymer type, thickness, plasticizer level, and permeability govern whether water ingress occurs by diffusion or through pores. Semi-permeable coatings can allow core hydration while staying intact, giving swollen cores and sustained or osmotic-type release. Insufficient pore-former in coatings or small coating porosity can delay drug exit until rupture or slow diffusion through the gel.
- Osmotic systems/orifice effects: For controlled osmotic devices, membrane thickness and orifice diameter directly control release. Small or clogged orifices (or insufficient pore-former) produce lag or incomplete release; membrane permeability governs whether core swelling leads to pump-like release or membrane rupture.
- Agitation and medium composition: Dissolution hydrodynamics (agitation speed, apparatus type) and medium surfactant/pH significantly affect wetting, gel erosion, and fragment settling—higher agitation or surfactants typically accelerate erosion and reduce fragment suspension time.
These general relationships are well-documented across matrix, coated-pellet and osmotic formulations in the pharmaceutical literature.

Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - HPMC (hydroxypropyl methylcellulose) viscosity and grade: multiple studies (e.g., Siepmann & Peppas and related matrix literature) show that higher-viscosity HPMC forms a stronger, more coherent gel layer on hydration. That gel layer both slows water penetration and reduces erosion, shifting the dominant release mechanism toward diffusion through a viscous gel and away from rapid disintegration. Lower-viscosity HPMC hydrates and erodes faster, producing faster and more erosion-controlled release. - Hydrophobic excipients and fillers: inclusion of waxes/beeswax/glyceryl behenates or long-chain triglycerides decreases tablet/pellet wettability and water uptake, reduces swelling and porosity, and slows dissolution/disintegration. Higher proportions of hydrophobic excipients often produce delayed or incomplete water ingress and can support an intact outer shell while the inner core slowly hydrates. - Film/coating composition and thickness: water-insoluble but permeable coatings (or semi-permeable cellulose acetate type coatings) can behave like a bag: they allow water ingress but resist rupture. Thicker coatings and lower permeability (lower pore fraction) increase lag times and can prevent fragmentation; more plasticizer usually increases flexibility but also permeability, influencing whether the film fractures or remains intact as a bag. - Osmotic/“push” type behavior: in systems with a permeable coating and a swellable core (or a push layer), water influx can create core swelling and pressure. If the coating is intact and has only small orifice(s), release can be primarily osmotic (zero-order) through an orifice; if no orifice or if orifice is blocked, pressure may be relieved by slow diffusion through the coating or by eventual coating rupture. Orifice diameter is a critical determinant of release rate in osmotic systems: smaller orifices reduce rate and increase sensitivity to blockage. - Gel layer buoyancy and suspension: strong, hydrated HPMC gels have low apparent density and high viscosity — hydrated fragments/pellets may be neutrally buoyant or slow to settle and can remain suspended, especially in low-agitation conditions or in media with surfactants that reduce surface tension. - Agitation and medium effects: dissolution hydrodynamics (paddle speed, apparatus type) profoundly affect both physical disintegration (coating rupture/fragmentation) and the convective transport of dissolved drug through a gel layer. Increased agitation tends to accelerate erosion/fragmentation and increases apparent dissolution rate for diffusion-limited systems.
Tentative Mechanistic Interpretation for the Current Product (Observed phenomena → plausible formulation/process factors → likely effects on release; hypotheses only) 1) Film coating remains intact while core swells and a gel layer is present - Hypothesis: the coating is water-permeable but mechanically robust (or too thick), so water enters but the film does not rupture. The core probably contains a high-viscosity HPMC (or similar swellable polymer) and/or hydrophobic excipients that slow internal erosion. - Consequence for release: drug release is likely governed by diffusion through the gel layer and/or permeation through the coating (possibly giving an apparent lag or slowly rising release). If core swelling builds pressure but cannot rupture the coating, release may remain diffusion-limited or show an eventual burst if/when the coating fails. 2) Swollen fragments remain suspended for long periods - Hypothesis: the gelled fragments have low apparent density and high viscosity and are not overcome by gravitational settling under the chosen agitation. Alternatively, the formulation contains low-density excipients (e.g., lipidic components) that reduce fragment density. - Consequence for release: suspension of swollen fragments can create a persistent viscous microenvironment around particles, reducing convective renewal and slowing mass transfer; measured release may be reduced and show high variability depending on agitation and vessel geometry. 3) Fragmentation behavior inconsistent or delayed - Hypothesis: a combination of a cohesive gel-forming polymer (high-MW HPMC), relatively low erosion tendency (low soluble filler), and a flexible, impermeable/flexible film coating (possibly over-plasticized or thick) prevents normal disintegration. If the process used low mechanical stress (e.g., soft compaction) the pellet mechanical strength may be high. - Consequence for release: slower, potentially non-zero-order release with sensitivity to hydrodynamic conditions; under in vivo conditions (different shear and transit) release could differ markedly from in vitro.
Limitations in the evidence - The above associations (HPMC viscosity → gel strength → slower release; hydrophobic excipients → reduced water uptake; orifice size → osmotic flux) are well supported in the matrix and osmotic literature, but without specific formulation details (polymer type and molecular weight, coating composition and thickness, plasticizer level, excipient identities and amounts, orifice presence/diameter, and process parameters) these remain hypotheses rather than confirmed mechanisms for the current product. - There is limited ability to distinguish between an intentional semi-permeable coated osmotic-like product and an intact non-rupturing diffusion-limited coated multiparticulate without targeted experiments.
Suggestions for Further Experiments or Validation Prioritize experiments that differentiate diffusion-limited vs. pressure/rupture-driven behavior and that identify the roles of polymer viscosity, hydrophobic content, coating permeability, and hydrodynamics.
Quick diagnostics (fast, informative) - Visual dissolution with video/microscopy: record pellets during dissolution to see whether coating remains intact, if or when ruptures occur, and how fragments behave. Use different paddle speeds (50 → 150 rpm) and APS (Apparatus 1 vs 2/3/4) to test hydrodynamic sensitivity. - Water uptake / swelling kinetics: measure mass increase of single pellets over time in dissolution medium to quantify water uptake rate and maximum swelling. - Porosity and density: determine tapped and true density of fragments and swollen pellets to evaluate why fragments remain suspended. - Simple solvent permeability test on coatings: measure weight gain or tracer uptake of coated pellets in water and in media with surfactants. - Orifice check (if osmotic-like system suspected): inspect for drilled/formed orifice(s); measure diameter and test whether orifice becomes blocked by gel during dissolution.
Formulation/process variation (definitive mechanistic tests) - Change HPMC viscosity/grade in core (or comparable swellable polymer) while keeping other variables constant: expect lower-viscosity grades to erode faster and produce faster release and more fragmentation. - Reduce hydrophobic excipient fraction or replace with more water-soluble filler: expect increased water uptake, faster disintegration, and faster/more reproducible release. - Modify coating thickness/permeability: thinner or more permeable coatings should reduce lag and allow earlier fragmentation or release; increase plasticizer only if mechanical brittleness is causing premature rupture — but plasticizer also increases permeability. - Agitation and medium changes: test with increased paddle speed and with addition of surfactant (e.g., 0.02–0.5% SLS) to probe whether poor wetting or low hydrodynamics cause the slow/variable release. - Use USP Apparatus 4 (flow-through cell) for suspending fragile/lowdensity fragments and better control of hydrodynamics; compare to USP 2 and 1. - Measure drug release kinetics under sink vs. non-sink conditions to rule out solubility-limited release due to gel-layer saturation.
Analytical/characterization suggestions - Cross-section imaging (SEM) before and after hydration to visualize coating integrity, gel layer thickness, pore formation. - Mechanical testing of coating (tensile/flexural) and core strength to see if coating can withstand internal swelling pressures. - Confocal Raman/FTIR mapping to assess polymer distribution and potential phase separation (e.g., hydrophobic islands). - Swelling pressure measurement (if available) to determine whether core expansion could rupture coating if coating were weaker/thinner.
How to interpret outcomes - If reducing HPMC viscosity or hydrophobic excipient leads to faster erosion and earlier fragmentation and a corresponding faster release, that supports the gel-stabilization/hydrophobic-wetting hypothesis. - If increasing agitation or adding surfactant accelerates release significantly, that points to hydrodynamic and wetting limitations (convective mass transfer or surface tension-mediated poor wetting) rather than an intrinsic membrane/osmotic mechanism. - If release remains slow and zero-order independent of these changes and there is a clear orifice, an osmotic mechanism with controlled orifice-driven release is more likely.
Summary - The most plausible, literature-supported explanation for an intact film with a swollen gelled core and suspended fragments is a combination of (a) a high-viscosity/gel-forming polymer in the core (strong HPMC gel), (b) hydrophobic excipients or low wettability that slow water ingress/erosion, and/or (c) a coating that is permeable but mechanically robust (or thick), producing diffusion-limited or osmotic-like behavior rather than rapid disintegration. These factors would cause slow, hydrodynamically-sensitive release and suspension of gelled fragments. The hypotheses above are consistent with published mechanisms but require targeted experiments (water uptake, agitation dependence, HPMC grade and hydrophobic excipient substitution, coating permeability/thickness tests, microscopy) to confirm which factor(s) dominate for the current product.

Literature‑Supported Typical Mechanisms - HPMC (and other hydrophilic matrix polymers): polymer viscosity grade and concentration strongly influence swelling, gel strength, and drug diffusion. Higher viscosity grades and higher polymer loadings produce thicker, more coherent gel layers with lower effective drug diffusion coefficients and slower erosion; lower viscosity grades hydrate faster but form weaker gels that erode/disintegrate sooner. These effects translate to longer lag times and slower sustained release as viscosity or polymer fraction increases.
- Hydrophobic excipients (e.g., magnesium stearate, stearic acids, glyceryl esters, talc): increasing levels reduce wettability and slow aqueous penetration into particles/tablets/pellets. That slows swelling and can preserve coating integrity longer, producing delayed or incomplete disintegration and suppressed initial release.
- Film/coating properties: coating thickness, polymer type (enteric vs. aqueous film former), plasticizer level and curing conditions govern permeability, brittleness, and tendency to crack. Thicker or less porous coatings and higher plasticizer content (in many systems) can prevent cracking and keep coatings intact, increasing lag time. Curing can densify a coating and reduce porosity/permeability, further delaying release. Conversely, low plasticizer or thin brittle coatings tend to crack and enable early release.

Run dissolution in multiple media (e.g., pH 1.2, 4.5, 6.8) with and without a surfactant (e.g., 0.1%–0.5% SDS) and at multiple agitation speeds (50, 75, 100 rpm) to test sensitivity to wettability and shear. Compare cores made with different HPMC viscosity grades (low, medium, high) and different % polymer to see influence on gel formation and release.

LLM mechanistic interpretation Phenomenon Review The key observations are: (a) the outer film/coating remains visually intact for a prolonged period while the tablet/particle core underneath swells substantially, (b) swollen core material fragments but those fragments remain suspended (do not rapidly disintegrate or fully erode) and persist in the dissolution medium, and (c) a continuous gel/viscoelastic layer is present around/within the core. In short, the system appears to take up water and form a strong geled/swollen core while the surface barrier remains cohesive, producing suspended gel fragments and extended retention of mass rather than rapid breakdown.
Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - HPMC (hydroxypropyl methylcellulose) viscosity grade and grade-dependent behavior: higher-viscosity HPMC yields a stronger, more cohesive gel layer that swells but resists erosion; this tends to slow release and favor diffusion-controlled kinetics, whereas lower-viscosity grades hydrate and erode faster (literature on hydrophilic matrix systems; Siepmann/Peppas-type analyses).
- Polymer fraction and matrix integrity: higher % polymer (e.g., HPMC fraction) increases gel strength and reduces fragmentation/erosion; lower polymer or inclusion of more soluble excipients increases disintegration.
- Hydrophobic excipients and lubricants: presence of hydrophobic binders/fillers (e.g., waxes, glyceryl behenates, hydrogenated vegetable oils, high amounts of Mg-stearate) lowers water uptake and can create a more cohesive, slower-wetting interior or reduce matrix porosity — delaying disintegration and causing sustained fragment suspension.
- Film coating properties: coating polymer/type, thickness and permeability determine water ingress and lag. Impermeable or low-porosity coatings (or cured coatings that lose porosity) permit slow, limited water uptake and can maintain surface integrity while interior swells. Plasticizer level affects film flexibility and crack formation; underplasticized films tend to stay intact but can delaminate or fracture in a different manner.
- Osmotic systems and orifice effects: in osmotic tablets a properly sized orifice controls release; too small or absent orifice (or occluded orifice/coating pores) leads to very slow or irregular release. Conversely, if the membrane is semi-permeable but no effective channel opens, the core may swell and fragment without continuous solute outflow.
- Agitation, medium composition and surface tension: low hydrodynamic stress and media lacking surfactants favor retention of gel fragments (they don’t break off/erode), while higher agitation or surfactant-containing media increase wetting, erosion and release.
- Particle size/porosity and manufacturing process: dense compacts, high compression forces, or low tablet porosity reduce penetration of dissolution medium; spray-coating process parameters (spray rate, inlet temperature, curing) influence coating porosity/permeability and thus water ingress.

If this is an osmotic design, an occluded/small orifice or low membrane porosity could convert intended osmotic pumping into swelling-limited, fragment-shedding behavior and unpredictable release.
These are hypotheses based on typical effects reported in the literature; they are not validated conclusions for this specific product because critical formulation and process data (polymer grade/concentration, hydrophobic excipient levels, coating recipe and thickness, orifice presence/size, manufacturing conditions) are not provided.

- Water uptake/swelling and erosion tests: gravimetric measurement of weight gain and remaining mass vs time; rheology or texture analysis of the gel layer to quantify gel strength.
- Coating permeability and integrity: water vapor transmission or dye penetration tests; measure coating thickness and look for cracking/pores before and after curing.
- Composition checks: quantify hydrophobic excipients (waxes, lipids) and HPMC grade/DS/Mw; check plasticizer content.
- Dissolution/profiling experiments (comparative): run standard dissolution in multiple conditions to probe mechanism:
- Vary agitation (e.g., 50, 75, 100 rpm in USP II) to see shear dependence.
- Use media of different pH (1.2, 4.5, 6.8) and with/without surfactant (e.g., 0.1% SDS) to probe wettability effects.

- Release mechanism fitting: fit dissolution data to models (zero/first-order, Higuchi, Korsmeyer–Peppas) to distinguish diffusion vs erosion control.
- Manipulation experiments (formulation/process levers): small-scale formulation variants to test causes:
- Reduce HPMC viscosity or polymer fraction — expect faster erosion and less persistent fragments if gel strength is the cause.
- Reduce hydrophobic excipient levels or replace with more water-soluble excipients (mannitol, PEG) or add pore formers to coating — should increase water ingress and increase fragmentation and release.
- Modify coating porosity or thickness (reduce thickness or incorporate water‑soluble pore formers/plasticizer) or intentionally create an orifice if osmotic mechanism intended — should reduce lag and allow continuous release.
- Increase curing carefully or alter plasticizer content to see effect on film porosity and flexibility.

These behaviours indicate substantial water ingress into the dosage form (core swelling and gel formation) without corresponding rupture or dispersion of the outer layer, and a slow or incomplete disintegration/erosion process that produces buoyant or slowly-settling fragments.
Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - Hydrophilic matrix-formers (HPMC) create a viscous gel layer on hydration. The viscosity/grade and polymer concentration strongly influence hydration, gel strength and erosion: higher-viscosity grades and higher polymer fraction produce thicker, stronger gels that slow diffusion and resist mechanical breakup, often reducing disintegration and slowing release (classical Siepmann/Peppas and Colombo-type findings).
- Hydrophobic excipients (waxes, long-chain glycerides, high levels of lipids) reduce water penetration, create hydrophobic microdomains, and increase structural integrity of fragments; they can make matrices fragment into low-erosion, slowly-dispersing pieces. Several formulation studies show that increasing hydrophobic fraction decreases erosion rate and promotes intact fragments or persistent particulates.
- Coating characteristics (polymer type, thickness, plasticizer level) determine whether a coating will stretch/rupture or remain intact while permitting water permeation. Semi-permeable coatings used in osmotic systems allow water ingress but prevent outward erosion; without a designed orifice, internal swelling may occur without immediate release. More elastic/ductile films (higher plasticizer content or crosslinked/entangled polymers) resist splitting and remain intact under swelling.
- Osmotic/semipermeable systems and push–pull tablets are known to allow core swelling under an intact skin; release then depends on orifice size/formation. Small or occluded orifices severely retard exit of dissolved drug despite swelling.
- Agitation and medium composition (pH, surfactant) affect detachment/erosion of gel layers and wetting of hydrophobic domains; low agitation or absence of surfactant promotes persistence of swollen fragments and low apparent release. These are consistent findings across dissolution methodology studies.

Observed phenomenon → Possible formulation/process factors → Possible release behavior - Intact film while core swells → coating polymer is relatively impermeable (low water permeability), or coating has been over-cured/has low plasticizer content; or coating is enteric/insoluble at test pH → delayed release/lag time until coating becomes permeable or ruptures; potential for sudden release if the coating eventually fails (dose-dumping risk). - Clear gel layer beneath intact coating → core contains a high fraction of hydrophilic matrix polymer (e.g., high-viscosity HPMC) that swells into a strong gel → controlled diffusion-limited release while coating remains intact; if gel layer cannot escape through the coating, internal pressure may build causing later rupture or incomplete release if coating never opens. - Fragments remain suspended for long periods → fragments have low wetting (hydrophobic excipients) or low density (entrapped air) and/or the gel layer confers buoyancy/viscosity that resists erosion; agitation may be insufficient → incomplete or very slow dissolution/erosion, non-sink conditions at particle surface, and possibly a prolonged tail in release profile. - If system resembles an osmotic device but no clear orifice → either the orifice is too small/blocked, or the coating acts as a semi-permeable membrane; swelling without steady release indicates osmotic inflow without outflow pathway or with insufficient permeability. 2. Limitations of the literature / uncertainty - Direct one-to-one mapping of the observed behavior to specific formulation attributes requires knowledge of exact excipient identities, polymer grades, coating composition, coating weight gain, and manufacturing conditions. Published effects are general and depend on quantitative proportions and processing (e.g., spray conditions, curing). Where specific product details are not available, these remain plausible hypotheses rather than validated mechanisms.
Suggestions for Further Experiments or Validation Priority diagnostic experiments (fast, high information yield) 1. Dissolution conditions variation - Run dissolution in multiple media (pH 1.2, 4.5, 6.8) and with/without surfactant (e.g., 0.1–0.2% SDS) and at different agitation rates (50, 75, 100 rpm). Rationale: test if coating is pH-dependent (enteric) or if poor wetting/low agitation causes the suspended fragments and slow release. 2. Visual / imaging tests - Cross-sectioning and optical/SEM imaging of wetted units at time points to inspect coating integrity, penetration, and gel layer thickness. Micro-CT can non-destructively show internal swelling/voids and whether an orifice exists/opens. 3. Remove coating and test core alone - Manually remove the film from a subset of units and run dissolution of the bare core. If the core alone shows normal/expected release while the coated unit is delayed, the coating is the main barrier. 4. Coating characterization - Determine coating composition, thickness/weight gain, plasticizer level, and perform water vapor permeability or dye-uptake tests to estimate permeability. If coating is overcured, DS C or film mechanical tests can reveal embrittlement. 5. Polymer/excipient influence - Prepare small comparative batches or lab-scale compacts varying HPMC grade (e.g., K4M vs K15M), polymer:drug ratio, and hydrophobic excipient level to see effects on swelling, gel strength, and release. 6. Orifice / osmotic checks - If an osmotic design is suspected, inspect for the presence and size of any orifice (microscopy, microtomy). If present but small/blocked, cleaning or controlled enlargement can be tested in vitro. 7. Wetting/surfactant effect - Measure contact angle on the formulation surface and perform dissolution with added surfactant; a big change suggests wettability is limiting release. 8. Swelling and erosion metrics - Quantify swelling index (mass/volume gain over time) and mass loss (erosion) of cores/coated units to separate diffusion-controlled vs erosion-controlled release mechanisms. Use UV or HPLC assays to detect sudden bursts vs steady-state release. - Raman mapping or imaging to see API distribution pre- and post-wetting. Concurrently, inspect coating integrity (microscope/SEM) and measure gel layer thickness after hydration. LLM mechanistic interpretation Phenomenon Review - Key observations: the coated multiparticulates/pellets show a clearly swollen core while the external film coat remains largely intact for an extended period; fragmented pieces (film-coated fragments or pellets) remain suspended in the medium rather than rapidly disintegrating; a continuous gel/viscoelastic layer is observed at the pellet surface during hydration. Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - HPMC (hypromellose) viscosity and gel behavior: literature consistently reports that higher-viscosity HPMC grades (K15M, K100M) form stronger, more cohesive gel layers on hydration that resist erosion and slow drug diffusion; lower-viscosity grades (K4M, K15) hydrate and disentangle faster, leading to quicker erosion or higher diffusivity through the gel. Gel strength and thickness scale with polymer molecular weight/concentration and coating mass. - Hydrophobic excipients in core or coat: inclusion of hydrophobic materials (waxes, glyceryl behenates, hydrogenated vegetable oil, high levels of cetyl alcohol) reduces water ingress, promotes limited swelling but slows disintegration and drug release. Hydrophobic binders can cause cohesive swollen cores that do not fragment easily. - Coating composition and plasticizer level: plasticizers increase film flexibility; excessive plasticizer can prevent film cracking (keeping film intact) while too little plasticizer makes coats brittle and prone to fracture. Pore formers (PEG, PVP, HPC) increase permeability and accelerate release when included in coating formulations. - Osmotic systems and orifice size: in osmotic-controlled pellets (mini-osmotic pumps), water influx builds internal pressure; release rate depends on orifice size and coating permeability. Small orifices delay onset/limit flux until pressure or localized failure occurs; larger orifices allow more immediate controlled release. Impermeable or low-permeability coatings can give long lag times. - Agitation and hydrodynamics: reduced shear in USP dissolution tests favors intact gel-layer maintenance and floating/suspension of fragments; increased agitation promotes film rupture, erosion of gel layers and higher apparent release rates. - Mechanistic distinctions: intact gel-coated, swollen cores indicate diffusion-controlled release through a hydrated polymer network and/or limited pore-mediated permeation rather than rapid disintegration/erosion-controlled release seen when films rupture or erode.

If agitation or media changes increase film stress/permeation, an accelerated release or abrupt increase (if the film ruptures) is expected. - Alternative contributing factors to consider: excessive film thickness, high level of plasticizer preventing cracking, coating curing or crosslinking that reduces coating permeability, or presence of pH-dependent excipients where current medium pH reduces solubility/permeation.
Suggestions for Further Experiments or Validation Prioritize experiments that distinguish diffusion-through-gel vs film-rupture/erosion mechanisms and identify formulation or process levers.
Simple in vitro tests
Dissolution with varied agitation: run USP II at low (50 rpm), medium (75 rpm), and high (100–150 rpm) speeds. If release increases markedly with agitation, mechanical resistance of the film is a key factor.
Media variation: test in media with/without surfactant (e.g., 0.1% SDS or 0.5% Tween 80), across pH range (pH 1.2, 4.5, 6.8). Increased release with surfactant suggests hydrophobic barriers limiting wetting/permeation.
Flow-through (USP 4) test: can reveal whether continuous shear/flow accelerates erosion or pore-mediated release versus batch tests.
Characterization of coat and cores
SEM imaging (dry and after hydration) to inspect coating integrity, presence of pores, crack formation, and core swelling morphology.
Measure coating thickness and uniformity (microscopy or cross-section imaging).
Water uptake/swelling kinetics: gravimetric uptake of individual pellets over time; correlate swelling with drug release.
Mechanical testing: puncture/tensile testing of isolated films (if possible) to assess flexibility/brittleness and effect of plasticizer.
Porosity/permeability: mercury porosimetry or gas adsorption, or simpler dye penetration tests to assess coating permeability.
Formulation/process probes (small-scale experiments)
Reduce or remove hydrophobic excipient levels in the core (or replace with more hydrophilic binders) and compare dissolution—if release accelerates, hydrophobic core is a contributor.
Modify HPMC viscosity/level in the coat or matrix (test lower-viscosity HPMC or lower coat weight) to see if gel resistance and lag reduce.
Add a low level of pore former (PEG 4000, PVP, or HPC) into the coating (e.g., 2–10% w/w) and assess whether permeability and initial release increase.
Adjust plasticizer level: test reduced plasticizer to see if controlled cracking increases release (careful: too little plasticizer can make coat brittle and lead to uncontrolled friability).
For osmotic designs: test enlarging/introducing an orifice of controlled diameter and observe change in onset and magnitude of release.
Analytical and imaging follow-up
Track drug distribution during dissolution (e.g., sampling and imaging by Raman mapping or fluorescence if possible) to determine whether drug diffuses through the gel or is released after film failure.
Monitor particle size distribution post-hydration to quantify fragmentation vs intact particles.
If literature evidence appears limited for exact materials/process used here (e.g., proprietary polymer blends or unusual hydrophobic excipients), explicitly test the most likely variables first: coating permeability (pore-former, coat weight), polymer viscosity, hydrophobic excipient content, and agitation. The quickest discriminating experiments are agitation sensitivity, surfactant-containing media, and simple SEM + water uptake studies.

Gel viscosity and surface tension effects can prevent rapid settling. Surfactant concentration in medium influences whether fragments disperse or stay aggregated.
- Osmotic systems/orifice dependence: In osmotic delivery devices, small orifice size or temporary blockage by gel/particulates can produce prolonged lag times or incomplete release until the orifice opens or is cleared. Gel formation at the exit port can plug flow.

Reduce HPMC viscosity or content, or replace with a lower viscosity grade to weaken the gel barrier and promote faster erosion/disintegration (test in head‑to‑head dissolution).

Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - Hydrophilic matrix polymers (HPMC and related cellulose ethers): these hydrate on contact with aqueous media to form a viscous gel layer. Higher-viscosity grades (e.g., K15M/K100M type) form stronger, more cohesive gels that slow erosion and can maintain an intact surface film for long periods; lower viscosities hydrate faster and erode more readily. The literature routinely links increased HPMC viscosity and/or higher polymer loading with slower disintegration and sustained release due to gel-layer formation and reduced diffusion rates. - Hydrophobic excipients and lubricants: incorporation of hydrophobic lipids (waxes, glyceryl behenate, stearic acid) or high levels of hydrophobic lubricants (magnesium stearate) reduces wettability and water penetration. This can produce delayed swelling of the core, reduce particle breakup and favor intact pellets or agglomerates. Several studies report that relatively small fractions of hydrophobes can markedly change disintegration. - Film-coating properties (thickness, plasticizer content, curing): thicker coatings, lower film porosity, and coatings with high plasticizer levels or poor curing can resist cracking during core swelling. A flexible, intact film can accommodate core expansion and prevent shell rupture; conversely, brittle films or insufficient plasticizer often fracture, allowing rapid release. The literature emphasizes that coating mechanical properties (tensile strength, elongation, Tg) strongly influence whether films hold or break during hydration. - Osmotic/semipermeable shell behavior: semipermeable coatings that allow water ingress but restrict solute egress (and lack an appropriately sized orifice) will permit core swelling under osmotic pressure without immediate release — the core swells while the outer film stays intact. Studies of push–pull and elementary osmotic pump systems show that orifice size and permeability govern lag time and the onset of release. - Processing effects (pellet porosity, compression, spheronization): denser, less porous cores or those with low friability tend to resist disintegration even after significant water uptake. Spheronization parameters, binder level, and drying/cure conditions for pellets influence internal porosity and mechanical cohesion; the literature connects lower porosity/higher binding with prolonged integrity on hydration. - Agitation and medium composition effects: many reports note that low hydrodynamic stress and absence of surfactants in the medium slow erosion and disintegration of gel-forming systems. Conversely, increased agitation or surfactants that improve wettability accelerate disintegration and drug release.

Intact film + swollen core → semipermeable coating or a highly cohesive HPMC-based outer layer with sufficient flexibility (high plasticizer or low Tg) and low porosity. Possible cause: designed/accidental use of a semipermeable polymer or dense film coat. Predicted release behavior: initial lag (water uptake without drug release), followed by either osmotic-driven extrusion if an orifice exists or an eventual burst if the film mechanically fails at higher swelling pressures. 2. Gel layer present → significant HPMC (or other hydrophilic binder) content in the core or coat, particularly a higher-viscosity grade, producing a viscous gel that inhibits particle break-up. Predicted release behavior: diffusion-controlled release through the gel (sustained) and slow erosion; dissolution rate strongly dependent on polymer viscosity and thickness. 3. Fragments remain suspended → partial erosion producing cohesive gel fragments whose density is near that of the medium (due to entrapped air or low-density excipients) or strong polymeric networks that do not disintegrate to fines. Possible cause: inclusion of hydrophobic excipient(s) that reduce wettability and particle fragmentation. Predicted release behavior: erratic or prolonged tailing in dissolution profiles; incomplete release under mild agitation. 4. Core clearly swollen while coat intact → either (a) semipermeable coating (osmotic mechanism) or (b) water ingress through micro-pores or defects rather than macroscopic cracks. Possible cause: small orifice(s) absent or too small, low coat permeability, or dense core that builds internal pressure without rupturing. Predicted release behavior: substantial lag time, then either a pressure-driven pulse if rupture occurs or slow zero-order release if a controlled orifice/porous pathway exists.
Important caveat: these are mechanistic hypotheses based on known relationships (polymer viscosity, hydrophobe content, coat properties, process-induced porosity). Without direct measurements (coat thickness, porosity, polymer grades, plasticizer content, orifice presence/size), these cannot be confirmed.

measure film thickness and porosity. - Mercury porosimetry or helium pycnometry to quantify core porosity and density. - Confocal laser scanning microscopy (using fluorescently labeled water or polymers) to visualize water penetration pathways. - Formulation/process trials: - Vary HPMC viscosity and content in cores (low vs high viscosity) in small-scale comparative dissolution studies — literature predicts higher viscosity → slower erosion and maintenance of gel-layer integrity. - Reduce or remove hydrophobic excipients/lubricants or replace with less hydrophobic alternatives and assess effect on disintegration/wettability. - Modify coating parameters: reduce coat thickness, increase coat permeability (add pore-formers or reduce polymer level), change plasticizer level, or cure conditions; then measure effect on film rupture and release. - Where an osmotic mechanism is suspected, deliberately create an orifice of controlled size (for a subset of pellets) and compare release; literature shows orifice diameter strongly affects lag and release rate. - Analytical endpoints to collect: cumulative % release vs time, lag time, erosion/disintegration kinetics, pellet integrity scoring, water uptake curves, imaging of microstructure, and mechanical properties of the film.

Solid fragments (pieces of matrix or core) appear to break off but remain suspended in the medium for an extended period rather than rapidly dissolving. A hydrated/gel layer forms at the tablet surface (indicative of a swellable polymer matrix), and overall release appears prolonged and limited by these physical states.
Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - Swellable hydrophilic matrices (especially HPMC) form a hydrated gel layer on contact with aqueous medium; the properties of that gel (thickness, viscosity, mechanical strength) control drug release by a combination of diffusion through the gel and erosion of the outer layer. Higher polymer viscosity/grade and higher polymer fraction -> stronger, thicker gel, slower diffusion and slower erosion; lower viscosity/grade -> thinner, more rapidly eroding gel and faster release (Siepmann & Peppas-type models; many matrix-release studies).
- Hydrophobic excipients (waxes, long-chain fatty acids/esters, ethylcellulose) reduce water uptake, reduce gel formation or slow hydration, and increase the contribution of pore diffusion rather than matrix swelling—leading to slower uptake and slower disintegration.
- Film coatings that are semi-permeable (e.g., ethylcellulose, cellulose acetate) or otherwise low-porosity can allow the core to hydrate and swell without coating rupture; release is then controlled by diffusion through the film or by osmotic pressure forcing drug out via defects/orifices. The presence and amount of pore-formers/plasticizer and the coating thickness strongly affect permeability and the tendency of the film to crack/rupture during core swelling or curing.
- In multiparticulate or fragmented systems, detached pieces may remain suspended if they are buoyant or entrained in a viscous gel; poor wetting or low solubility of API can also make fragments persist. Agitation (hydrodynamics) and medium composition (surfactants, ionic strength) markedly change fragment dissipation and measured release.
- In osmotic or controlled-orifice systems, the orifice size critically determines the rate at which swollen core or dissolved drug exits; a too-small orifice can cause delayed or incomplete release despite core hydration. Conversely, a too-large orifice may permit rapid release or mechanical loss of swollen material.

Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - HPMC (hydroxypropyl methylcellulose) viscosity and concentration - Higher-viscosity HPMC grades and higher HPMC content form thicker, more robust gel layers on hydration, slow polymer chain disentanglement and erosion, and reduce diffusion rates of dissolved drug through the gel. This generally leads to slower, more erosion-resistant release (Siepmann & Peppas-type findings). - Hydrophobic excipients (waxes, glyceryl esters, hydrogenated oils, hydrophobic stearates) - Adding hydrophobic fillers/lipids to a matrix reduces wettability and water uptake, encourages formation of coherent fragments rather than rapid disintegration, and can increase buoyancy or suspension time of fragments. Literature-Supported Typical Mechanisms - Hydrophilic matrix polymers (e.g., HPMC, PEO): viscosity grade and polymer content strongly influence water uptake, gel strength and erosion. Higher-viscosity grades (HPMC K100M vs K4M, PEO 7·10^6 vs 3·10^6) form thicker, stronger gel layers that slow diffusion and erosion; lower-viscosity grades hydrate faster but are more prone to erosion and faster drug release. (General pharmaceutics literature and dissolution studies.) - Hydrophobic excipients/lipids (waxes, glyceryl behenate, long-chain triglycerides): increasing the fraction of hydrophobic excipients reduces water ingress, creates tortuous pores, and retards disintegration and release; they tend to promote sustained release and can cause intact-coated behavior if present at the surface.

Thicker, less permeable films or films that have been overcured/crosslinked slow water penetration and keep fragments intact longer. Low plasticizer or brittle films may fracture into pieces, but those pieces can remain intact if the core is gummy.

If the orifice is occluded, the system may switch to diffusion through the membrane or eventual rupture.

Lower agitation often yields longer apparent lag and more persistent swollen fragments (USP dissolution method papers). - Combined outcomes: The literature supports that a combination of (a) a cohesive gel layer (from high-viscosity HPMC or high polymer content), (b) hydrophobic excipients reducing wettability, and/or (c) a low‑permeability/over-thick coating or small/plugged orifice will produce the observed pattern: intact outer film for a long time, core swelling/gel formation, suspended fragments, and delayed/incomplete release.

On wetting, this forms a cohesive gel that swells but resists erosion; pieces remain as coherent, buoyant/suspended fragments. The coating may be water‑insoluble / low‑permeability or of sufficient thickness to create a lag, so only limited hydration of the core occurs and the core surface swells locally into gel but the rest remains relatively dry. This can produce swollen fragments that do not disintegrate fully and yield incomplete/retarded release. - Hypothesis C — Partial plug/blockage of designed outlet (if an osmotic/pump-type device): If the product relies on an aperture for release, a too‑small or partially blocked orifice will let ingress occur very slowly, causing the core to swell behind the intact film rather than releasing drug. Literature on osmotic systems shows orifice sizing critically controls rate and onset. - Hypothesis D — Process-related binder or lubricant overuse: Excess lubricant (e.g., magnesium stearate) or a strong binder in granulation can make granules/tablets more cohesive and hydrophobic, causing slow breakup and persistent fragments. Chain of reasoning (observations → likely design/process factors → expected release behaviour): - Observation: Intact coating + swollen core → Factor: low coating permeability, thick coating, or hydrophobic surface agents limiting water entry → Release behaviour: lag time followed by erratic or slow release. - Observation: Gel layer and suspended fragments → Factor: high-viscosity HPMC or high polymer load with insufficient erosion-promoting excipients → Release behaviour: sustained/extended but possibly incomplete release; particles remain as slowly eroding gels. - Observation: Fragments remain suspended and do not disperse → Factor: hydrophobic excipients or low-density ingredients (air entrainment), or highly cohesive matrix → Release behaviour: low surface area for dissolution, hence delayed/attenuated release. Note: These are plausible mechanisms supported generally in the literature but require product‑specific confirmation.
Suggestions for Further Experiments or Validation Priority experiments to differentiate hypotheses and guide corrective actions: 1. Simple dissolution modifications - Run USP II dissolution at multiple agitation speeds (50, 75, 100 rpm) and compare release and fragment behaviour. If higher agitation speeds reduce lag and promote fragmentation, mechanical resistance (gel cohesion) and hydrodynamics are contributors. - Test dissolution in different media (0.1 N HCl, pH 6.8 buffer, and media with surfactant e.g., 0.1–0.2% SDS or 0.05% Tween 80). Improved release with surfactant suggests wettability limitations from hydrophobic excipients or coating. 2. Visual/physical characterization during dissolution - Time‑lapse optical imaging or video of dosage form in dissolution medium to document ingress points, gel layer formation, and fragment detachment. - Measure gel layer thickness and mass gain (water uptake) at defined time points (gravimetric swelling test). Compare to reference formulations with known HPMC grades. 3. Microscopy and structure analysis - Cross‑sectional optical microscopy/SEM of dosage form before and after limited exposure to medium to see coating integrity, ingress channels, and internal swelling/porosity. - Micro-CT imaging to visualize internal swelling, porosity changes, and possible air pockets or channels. 4. Composition and process checks - Quantify hydrophobic excipient levels (lipids, stearates) in core and compare with formulations known to disintegrate normally. - Check coating thickness and permeability (e.g., water vapor transmission or dissolution-coating permeability tests). If coating is thicker or less permeable than expected, consider reducing thickness or using a more permeable polymer or more plasticizer. - If product uses an orifice, confirm orifice diameter and check for blocking/occlusion. 5. Comparative formulation experiments - Make small-scale batches varying one factor at a time: HPMC grade (low vs high viscosity) and level, hydrophobic excipient content, coating thickness and polymer type. Run parallel dissolution and visual tests. 6. Mechanistic assays - Water uptake kinetics and dynamic swelling/erosion profiling (measure mass loss and gel strength). - Mechanical integrity testing on swollen gels (texture analyser) to quantify gel cohesiveness and propensity to break up under shear. 7. Analytical confirmation - Assay for residual drug in fragments vs dissolved fraction over time to determine whether drug is trapped in persistent gel fragments. - If suspected coating issues, solvent-extract coating and analyze composition (polymer/plasticizer content).
If literature evidence seems insufficient for a specific aspect (for example, exact behavior for a novel polymer blend or an unusual lipid excipient), explicitly run the comparative formulation experiments above and consider advanced imaging (confocal Raman mapping to localize drug/polymer) and biorelevant hydrodynamic testing (reciprocating cylinder or flow-through cell) to mimic in vivo conditions.
Summary - The combination of a cohesive gel-forming polymer (likely HPMC or similar), hydrophobic excipients or a low-permeability coating, and/or orifice/processing issues can explain an intact film with a swollen core and suspended fragments leading to delayed release. The literature supports each link in this chain, but product-specific experiments (dissolution under varied conditions, imaging, water uptake/gel strength, coating permeability and formulation variants) are necessary to confirm which factor(s) are dominant and to guide formulation or process remediation.

Lower viscosity grades hydrate faster but produce weaker gels that erode more readily, leading to faster release. - Hydrophobic excipients (lipids, waxes, long‑chain stearates): Increasing proportions of hydrophobic fillers or lubricants (e.g., glyceryl behenate, hydrogenated vegetable oil, stearic acid) reduces wettability and water uptake, retards swelling and erosion, and can promote formation of discrete swollen gelled particles rather than rapid disintegration. They can also make the internal matrix more mechanically coherent, helping fragments retain shape and suspend. - Film coatings / semipermeable membranes: A semipermeable coating (e.g., cellulose acetate) can remain intact while permitting water ingress; the core then swells under the intact film.
